title: Elaine Brooks: resection versus transplantation or ablation
fairness: Resection assessment is the best offered priority for this solitary peripheral tumor with preserved synthetic function, no supplied clinical evidence of significant portal hypertension, and a limited resection map. The tumor burden also makes transplant referral a plausible resident error rather than a random foil.

The resident must interpret reserve and portal-hypertension observations, then integrate tumor size and operative anatomy to rank the three treatments. The 4.6-cm size makes thermal ablation a less attractive competitor without inventing a new numerical rule.

The resection map is decision-critical feasibility information, not a sufficient answer by itself: poor reserve or portal hypertension could still change the priority. The three options name concrete treatments at the same assessment stage.

The explanation appropriately limits the answer to assessment rather than operative clearance. This standalone item is coherent. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally strong offered priority was identified; current guideline confirmation remains outside this offline review.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between tumor-burden eligibility and the best initial treatment assessment. Do not turn the explanation into a universal claim that transplantation or ablation is prohibited.
Preserve the raw reserve and portal-hypertension findings rather than replacing them with a resection-eligible label.

title: Omar Bennett: HCC with main portal-vein tumor occlusion
fairness: Medical-oncology assessment for systemic therapy is the best offered pathway. Macrovascular tumor extension changes the interpretation of an otherwise small tumor, and main portal occlusion creates a separate perfusion concern for routine chemoembolization.

The resident must interpret the vascular staging and then use portal perfusion plus preserved function/activity to rank systemic therapy, chemoembolization and standard transplantation. Patent hepatic arteries can tempt an embolization choice but do not resolve the portal-flow problem.

The supplied HCC diagnosis is legitimate for this management task. The word standard appropriately bounds the transplant comparison; it is not a rhetorical absolute or an independent nonmedical route to the key.

The explanation preserves the distinction between routine chemoembolization and specialist locoregional exceptions. This standalone case is coherent, and no confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. Exact current systemic regimens and selected-center exceptions were not verified offline.
suggestions: Keep the explicit tumor nature of the portal occlusion; changing it to an unspecified thrombus would materially change the staging inference.
Retain the limited claim about routine chemoembolization and standard transplantation rather than generalizing to all arterial treatments or all transplant protocols.

cues.phrase: after colon resection and completion of an outside course of systemic therapy
cues.why: Together with all lesions decreasing and the fully supplied operation, this makes further systemic therapy look like repeating a completed step while the key follows the named next plan. This is a sequence cue, not a claim that further chemotherapy is clinically never useful.

fairness: HPB resection assessment is defensible. The lesion count and bilobar distribution do not alone exclude surgery; six lesions including a deep 5.2-cm target also make ablation less competitive.

The stated 45% is a constructed patient measurement, not proof of universally adequate functional reserve after chemotherapy. The assessment wording and later vascular review avoid a confident clinical error, but the explanation must not be read as operative clearance.

The later detailed outflow map can coherently reveal a new problem after an initial referral. This first node stands alone, but the present surgical solution and weak competitors make it a one-step referral match.
suggestions: Replace the statement that the operation encompasses all six sites with neutral distribution and remnant observations that the learner must use to evaluate complete clearance.

Ask a concrete unresolved decision at the same planning stage and compare credible strategies. Make number/distribution compete with a meaningful functional or technical constraint rather than merely supplying a finished operation.
Preserve the distinction between initial resection assessment and the later outflow-dependent operative decision; do not reveal the next node's problem in this node's feedback.

title: Lena Ortiz: segment IV drainage after middle hepatic-vein removal
clarityIssues: The remnant volume is unchanged from the earlier plan requires the previous exhibit. The current node does not restate the amount or functional distribution of remaining liver, so it does not fully stand alone.

Right hepatectomy with middle-hepatic-vein reconstruction names a specific operative strategy, while the explanation retreats to assessing whether reconstruction can preserve drainage. Those are different levels of commitment.

cues.phrase: The right-sided resection must include the middle hepatic vein.
cues.why: The key alone repeats middle-hepatic-vein and supplies a repair to the named structure; the alternatives concern portal flow or chemotherapy. With the task already announcing a new resectability problem, this permits a strong word-to-repair shortcut. The anatomical observation itself is necessary and should not simply be deleted.

fairness: There is a genuine two-step anatomical inference: identify dependence of retained segment IV on the vein being removed, then distinguish venous drainage from remnant volume and inflow. Portal embolization does not directly restore the lost venous outlet.

The map establishes an outflow concern but does not establish reconstructibility, the tributaries that can be preserved/reimplanted, or whether sufficient functional liver would remain if segment IV were sacrificed. I cannot confirm that the specifically named reconstruction is uniquely justified from these observations. This is an unresolved technical feasibility question, not an assertion that reconstruction is wrong.

The sequence is coherent as an escalation from initial assessment to a detailed vascular review, and prior feedback does not reveal the drainage answer. Independence is weakened by the reference to the earlier remnant plan.

Functional remnant outflow is high-yield general-surgery knowledge. Selecting this exact venous reconstruction from a sparse sectoral map is a more specialized HPB decision; highYield is false for the current exact task, not for the underlying outflow principle.
suggestions: Either ask which remnant functional problem requires resolution before surgery, using parallel competing planning actions, or supply a clinician-reviewed operative map sufficient to compare genuinely feasible operative strategies.
Make all choices operate at the same level of commitment. Do not key a definitive reconstruction while explaining only a need for feasibility assessment.

Restate the minimum relevant remnant information in the current update and make the anatomy, rather than a unique vein-name match, determine the decision. Have an HPB clinician resolve the exact reconstruction choice before retaining it as the key.

The task is complete and stands alone. The selected procedure and explicit branch map make it straightforward; translating a supplied segment set and recalling embolize-the-resection-side is not two consequential steps here.
Portal embolization and preservation of the future liver remnant are high-yield, but the second portal-target node repeats substantially the same operation-to-branch matching skill.
suggestions: Keep the procedure mechanism but make a real patient-specific anatomical discrepancy or competing remnant plan change the territory selected. Supply the actual observations needed to resolve it rather than withholding the portal map.
Avoid making the correct option a verbatim copy of the resection segment set. Have the learner infer a consequential remnant relationship, with clinically credible competing territories.
If retained as foundational anatomy practice instead, seek explicit acceptance of that easy role rather than describing it as a two-step resident challenge.

title: Marcus Lee: oncologic progression despite remnant growth

The update follows portal embolization coherently and supplies enough current information to stand alone. The favorable reserve conclusion is already given, so the learner does not independently interpret it; removing that row leaves the same key.

Remove the preceding explanation's direct rehearsal of the follow-up objective when revising that node, and reassess the complete sequence.

Contrast-enhanced ultrasound is a clinically credible comparator, so this is more demanding than a plainly excluded-test item.

The narrow case should not teach that every radiographically suspected, potentially resectable intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma universally requires preoperative biopsy. The explanation should bind the tissue recommendation to this patient's unresolved diagnostic pathway.
